'''Benjamin Todd <!-- NOTE: Do not add "Ben" here per [[WP:HYPOCORISM]]--> Roethlisberger Sr.''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|r|ɒ|θ|l|ᵻ|s|b|ɜːr|ɡ|ər}} {{respell|ROTH|liss|BUR|gur}}; born March 2, 1982), nicknamed "'''Big Ben'''", is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 18 seasons with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Miami RedHawks football|Miami RedHawks]], and was selected by the Steelers in the first round (11th overall) of the [[2004 NFL draft]].

Roethlisberger earned the [[AP NFL Rookie of the Year Award|AP NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year]] Award in 2004 and his first [[Pro Bowl]] selection in 2007. In 2006, he became the youngest [[Super Bowl]]–winning quarterback in NFL history, winning [[Super Bowl XL]] in his second season at the age of 23. Roethlisberger led the Steelers to a second Super Bowl title in four seasons in [[Super Bowl XLIII]]. In 2011, his third Super Bowl appearance, the Steelers lost in [[Super Bowl XLV]].

Roethlisberger was one of the most prolific passers in NFL history. Upon retirement, he ranked 5th all-time in NFL career passing yards (64,088),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pryor |first=Brooke |date=January 27, 2022 |title='Grateful' Roethlisberger retires after 18 seasons |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/33158955/pittsburgh-steelers-qb-ben-roethlisberger-retires-18-seasons |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220203221805/https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/33158955/pittsburgh-steelers-qb-ben-roethlisberger-retires-18-seasons |archive-date=February 3, 2022 |access-date=February 9, 2022 |website=[[ESPN.com]]}}</ref> 8th all-time in touchdowns (418), and 5th in completions (5,440) among quarterbacks with a minimum of 1,500 career attempts. He also had the fourth-highest career winning percentage (.710) as a starter in the regular season among quarterbacks with a minimum of 100 starts and was one of only six quarterbacks in NFL history to have beaten at least 31 of the current 32 NFL teams.<ref name="31 teams">{{cite web |last=Bryan |first=Dave |date=December 24, 2014 |title=Roethlisberger Sets New Franchise Passing Yardage Record, Joins 31-Club With Sunday Win |url=https://steelersdepot.com/2014/12/roethlisberger-sets-new-franchise-passing-yardage-record-joins-31-club-sunday-win/ |access-date=December 7, 2019 |website=Steelers Depot }}</ref>

Known for playing outside the [[passing pocket]] in what he calls "[[Street football (American)|backyard football]]",<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hartman |first=Jeff |date=November 9, 2017 |title=For Ben Roethlisberger and the Steelers, it is 'Dome sweet Dome' |url=https://www.behindthesteelcurtain.com/nfl-pittsburgh-steelers-news/2017/11/9/16626894/steelers-news-for-ben-roethlisberger-and-the-steelers-it-is-dome-sweet-dome-lucas-oil-stadium-nfl |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191207195258/https://www.behindthesteelcurtain.com/nfl-pittsburgh-steelers-news/2017/11/9/16626894/steelers-news-for-ben-roethlisberger-and-the-steelers-it-is-dome-sweet-dome-lucas-oil-stadium-nfl |archive-date=December 7, 2019 |access-date=December 7, 2019 |website=Behind the Steel Curtain|publisher=SB Nation |language=en}}</ref> Roethlisberger grew up idolizing [[John Elway]] and has often been compared to him, wearing number 7 in his honor.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cook |first=Ron |date=October 12, 2009 |title=Steelers' Roethlisberger shows flashes of Elway |url=http://www.post-gazette.com/steelers/2009/10/12/Steelers-Roethlisberger-shows-flashes-of-Elway/stories/200910120233 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131106005703/http://www.post-gazette.com/steelers/2009/10/12/Steelers-Roethlisberger-shows-flashes-of-Elway/stories/200910120233 |archive-date=November 6, 2013 |access-date=May 27, 2022 |website=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Villani |first=Jared |date=November 22, 2018 |title=Ben Roethlisberger Reveals Why He Wears No. 7 |url=https://clutchpoints.com/steelers-news-ben-roethlisberger-says-he-wears-no-7-because-of-hero-john-elway/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191217030413/https://clutchpoints.com/steelers-news-ben-roethlisberger-says-he-wears-no-7-because-of-hero-john-elway/ |archive-date=December 17, 2019 |access-date=December 17, 2019 |website=[[ClutchPoints]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Early life==
Roethlisberger was born in [[Lima, Ohio]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Robinson |first=Tom |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FxmDDwAAQBAJ&q=roethlisberger+lima+ohio+hometown&pg=PA16 |title=Ben Roethlisberger: Gifted and Giving Football Star |date=September 2012 |publisher=Enslow Publishers, Inc. |isbn=978-1-4645-0208-8 |language=en |access-date=May 1, 2022 |archive-date=May 1, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220501214756/https://books.google.com/books?id=FxmDDwAAQBAJ&q=roethlisberger+lima+ohio+hometown&pg=PA16 |url-status=live }}</ref> the son of Ida Jane (née Foust) and Kenneth Todd "Ken" Roethlisberger. His father is a former pitcher and quarterback at Georgia Tech.<ref>{{Cite web |last=O'Connor |first=Ian |date=February 1, 2006 |title=Roethlisberger uses TD passes to honor late mother |url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/columnist/oconnor/2006-02-01-oconnor-ben_x.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120630225021/http://www.usatoday.com/sports/columnist/oconnor/2006-02-01-oconnor-ben_x.htm |archive-date=June 30, 2012 |access-date=September 17, 2019 |website=USA Today}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Powell |first=Kimberly |date=May 23, 2019 |title=Ancestry of Ben Roethlisberger |url=http://genealogy.about.com/od/famous_family_trees/ss/ben-roethlisberger.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160107195557/http://genealogy.about.com/od/famous_family_trees/ss/ben-roethlisberger.htm |archive-date=January 7, 2016 |access-date=November 22, 2012 |website=ThoughtCo.}}</ref> He is of part Swiss descent; his surname, Roethlisberger (Swiss-German spelling: ''Röthlisberger''), is of Swiss origin, with roots in Geissbühl, a farming hamlet in the municipality of [[Lauperswil]], Switzerland.<ref>{{cite web |last=Fleming |first=David |date=January 19, 2005 |title=For whom the Ben tolls |url=https://www.espn.com/espn/print?id=1970310&type=story |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170926143441/https://www.espn.com/espn/print?id=1970310&type=story |archive-date=September 26, 2017 |access-date=November 12, 2019 |website=ESPN.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Roethlisberger discovers his Swiss roots |url=http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/dailycourier/news/s_451853.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071114061646/http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/dailycourier/news/s_451853.html |archive-date=November 14, 2007 |access-date=December 6, 2019 |website=PittsburghLIVE.com |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> His younger sister, Carlee Roethlisberger, played basketball for the [[University of Oklahoma]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Carlee Roethlisberger Profile |url=http://soonersports.com/sports/w-baskbl/mtt/roethlisberger_carlee00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111124002031/http://www.soonersports.com/sports/w-baskbl/mtt/roethlisberger_carlee00.html |archive-date=November 24, 2011 |access-date=December 11, 2011 |website=Oklahoma Sooners}}</ref>

At [[Findlay High School]] in [[Findlay, Ohio]], Roethlisberger was captain of the Trojans' [[high school football|football]], basketball, and baseball teams. Roethlisberger did not play quarterback until his senior year, giving way to the coach's son, Ryan Hite. Instead, Roethlisberger played [[wide receiver]]. "I'm a nationally known knucklehead in many people's eyes," Hite conceded in a 2004 interview to the ''[[Toledo Blade]]'', but insisted his decision had not been an act of [[nepotism]], or miscalculation.<ref name="tb1" /> "We did a bunch of drills and my son throwing to Ben was a better combination," he said.<ref name="tb1">{{cite web |last=Musselman |first=Ron |date=April 18, 2004 |title=Hindsight makes Hite's sight look blurry |url=http://www.toledoblade.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20040418/SPORTS09/40418012 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110208214750/http://www.toledoblade.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20040418%2FSPORTS09%2F40418012 |archive-date=February 8, 2011 |access-date=October 5, 2014 |website=Toledo Blade}}</ref>

Ken Roethlisberger, a former [[Georgia Tech]] quarterback, never publicly criticized Hite for playing Ryan ahead of his son Ben. He has stated, "It was a coach's call. You make good ones, you make bad ones. And I'm not even saying this was a bad one. We can say it was now, but how do we know for sure?" Ryan Hite went on to [[Denison Big Red|Denison University]] where, as a wide receiver, he set numerous career and single-season records by the time he graduated from college.<ref name="tb1" />

==College career==
[[File:Roethlisberger's number retired with Pont and Hitchens.jpg|thumb|Roethlisberger's [[Miami RedHawks football|Miami RedHawks]] jersey number being retired in 2007]]

===2000–2001===
{{See also|2001 Miami RedHawks football team}}
Roethlisberger played college quarterback at [[Miami University]] in [[Oxford, Ohio]]. After arriving at Miami in 2000, he was [[redshirt (college sports)|redshirt]]ed his first season.<ref>{{cite web |last=Myers |first=Massillon |date=September 6, 2019 |title=Freshman quarterback makes Miami Football history |url=http://www.oxfordobserver.org/article/freshman-quarterback-makes-history-at-first-miami-football-game |access-date=December 6, 2019 |website=Oxford Observer |archive-date=December 6, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191206042847/http://www.oxfordobserver.org/article/freshman-quarterback-makes-history-at-first-miami-football-game |url-status=live }}</ref> In the 2001 season, he made his collegiate debut against [[2001 Michigan Wolverines football team|Michigan]], completing 18 of 35 passes for 193 yards and two touchdowns in the 31–13 loss.<ref>{{cite web |title=Miami (OH) at Michigan Box Score, September 1, 2001 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2001-09-01-michigan.html |access-date=January 14, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |archive-date=January 15, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180115071557/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2001-09-01-michigan.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Against [[2001 Akron Zips football team|Akron]], he broke the school single-game passing record with 399 passing yards, with 70 of those yards coming on a Hail Mary to Eddie Tillitz to win the game by a score of 30–27 as time expired.<ref>{{cite web |title=Akron at Miami (OH) Box Score, October 13, 2001 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2001-10-13-miami-oh.html |access-date=January 14, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |archive-date=January 15, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180115002054/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2001-10-13-miami-oh.html |url-status=live }}</ref> When Miami played [[2001 Bowling Green Falcons football team|Bowling Green]], he had two touchdowns and 305 passing yards and broke the MAC freshman passing yardage record in the 24–21 victory.<ref>{{cite web |title=Miami (OH) at Bowling Green State Box Score, November 3, 2001 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2001-11-03-bowling-green-state.html |access-date=January 14, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |archive-date=January 15, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180115001546/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2001-11-03-bowling-green-state.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Against [[2001 Hawaii Warriors football team|Hawaii]], he broke school records for attempts, completions, and yardage, when he went 40 of 53 for 452 yards and three touchdowns in the 52–51 loss.<ref>{{cite web |title=Miami (OH) at Hawaii Box Score, November 17, 2001 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2001-11-17-hawaii.html |access-date=January 14, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |archive-date=January 15, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180115001630/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2001-11-17-hawaii.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He finished his first year with the Redhawks with 3,105 passing yards, 241 completions, and 25 touchdown completions while leading them to a 7–5 record.<ref name="muredhawks.com">{{cite web |title=Ben Roethlisberger Player Bio |url=http://www.muredhawks.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/roethlisberger_ben00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150630041550/http://www.muredhawks.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/roethlisberger_ben00.html |archive-date=June 30, 2015 |access-date=June 12, 2015 |website=Miami RedHawks}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2001 Miami (OH) RedHawks Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/miami-oh/2001-schedule.html |access-date=May 2, 2022 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=June 17, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170617202135/http://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/miami-oh/2001-schedule.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

===2002===
{{See also|2002 Miami RedHawks football team}}
Roethlisberger's second season as the RedHawks starter was marked with a 7–5 record once again.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2002 Miami (OH) RedHawks Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/miami-oh/2002-schedule.html |access-date=May 2, 2022 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=December 7, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191207195449/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/miami-oh/2002-schedule.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He broke the MAC single-game record for passing yards in a 48–41 loss against [[2002 Northern Illinois Huskies football team|Northern Illinois]] on October 12 when he threw for 525 yards and four touchdowns.<ref>{{cite web |title=Northern Illinois at Miami (OH) Box Score, October 12, 2002 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2002-10-12-miami-oh.html |access-date=January 14, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |archive-date=January 15, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180115001916/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2002-10-12-miami-oh.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He won the MAC East Special Teams Player of the Week for three punts that landed inside the 20 in the 27–13 victory over [[2002 Toledo Rockets football team|Toledo]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Miami (OH) at Toledo Box Score, October 26, 2002 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2002-10-26-toledo.html |access-date=January 14, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |archive-date=January 15, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180115071612/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2002-10-26-toledo.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=October 28, 2002 |title=MAC announces players of the week |url=https://getsomemaction.com/news/2002/10/28/FB_126092.aspx?path=football |access-date=May 27, 2022 |website=getsomemaction.com |language=en}}</ref> He established the Miami single-season record with 3,238 passing yards and 271 completions in 2002.<ref name="muredhawks.com" />

===2003===
{{See also|2003 Miami RedHawks football team}}
After starting the season with a loss to the [[Iowa Hawkeyes]], Roethlisberger led the Miami RedHawks to an unbeaten record in the MAC, 12 consecutive wins, a #10 ranking in the [[Associated Press]] poll, and a 49–28 victory over [[2003 Louisville Cardinals football team|Louisville]] in the [[2003 GMAC Bowl]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=GMAC Bowl – Miami (OH) vs Louisville Box Score, December 18, 2003 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2003-12-18-louisville.html |access-date=May 2, 2022 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=December 7, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191207195518/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2003-12-18-louisville.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=2003 Miami (OH) RedHawks Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/miami-oh/2003-schedule.html |access-date=December 7, 2019 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=December 7, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191207195257/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/miami-oh/2003-schedule.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He finished his 2003 season with a conference-leading 343 completions, 4,486 passing yards, and 37 passing touchdowns, breaking school single-season records in all three categories.<ref name="muredhawks.com" /> He was named as the MAC Offensive Player of the Year for the 2003 season.<ref>{{cite web |title=MAC Offensive Player of the Year Winners |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/awards/mac-opoy.html |access-date=March 27, 2018 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |archive-date=March 27, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180327085014/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/awards/mac-opoy.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

His jersey number 7 was retired by the RedHawks during homecoming on October 13, 2007; the festivities included the RedHawks football game against [[2007 Bowling Green Falcons football team|Bowling Green]]. Roethlisberger became the third athlete in Miami football history to have his number retired, joining [[John Pont]] and [[Bob Hitchens]]. Roethlisberger's number being retired was the first time in 34 years Miami retired a football jersey number.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 9, 2007 |title=A Battle of MAC Undefeateds as RedHawks Host Falcons in Homecoming Clash |url=http://muredhawks.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/100907aaa.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071012073157/http://muredhawks.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/100907aaa.html |archive-date=October 12, 2007 |access-date=December 11, 2011 |website=Miami RedHawks}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=October 10, 2007 |title=Miami to Honor Ben Roethlisberger and Terry Hoeppner at Football Game on Saturday |url=http://muredhawks.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/101007aac.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071212160045/http://muredhawks.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/101007aac.html |archive-date=December 12, 2007 |access-date=December 11, 2011 |website=Miami RedHawks}}</ref>
